blogs.title: The Split Shield: How *Pacito* Separates Presidential Power to Bar Entry from the Mandate to Support Those Already Inside
blogs.description: Analyzing the Ninth Circuit's novel approach to the litigation of the suspension of the refugee admissions program, this post examines the distinction the court draws between Presidential discretion under 8 U.S.C. 1182(f) regarding entry, and the statutory obligations imposed by INA 1522 regarding resettlement services. It explores how the court's stay order effectively limits executive power by requiring the government to reinstate services for those already admitted, even as it grants deference to the President's justification for barring future admissions. This analysis places the ruling within the broader context of the separation of powers in immigration law and the role of 1182(f) as a barrier that cannot be used to freeze statutory duties post-admission.

blogs.title: Authorization Versus Mandate: C.J. Lee's Textualist Dissent on the Nature of Refugee Resettlement Funding
blogs.description: A focused examination of Circuit Judge Lee's dissent regarding the legal nature of 8 U.S.C. 1522. This post highlights the textual battle between the concept of 'Authorization' versus 'Mandate' and analyzes the dissent's argument that subsections using 'shall' are qualified language for discretionary funding. Key issues include the definition of 'available appropriations' and the permissive nature of the Director's role in providing services. This blog piece discusses the implications of this textualist debate for statutory interpretation in administrative law and how it contrasts with the Majority's reading of the Refugee Act.

blogs.title: The Predictive Stay: What *Pacito*'s Interim Order Reveal About the 'Likely to Prevail' Factor in Immigration Litigation
blogs.description: This post investigates the procedural significance of the Ninth Circuit's decision to explicitly predict the likely outcome of the merits in a stay order vacating previous stays. Moving beyond standard stay factors (irreparable injury, balance of hardships), the order signals that the administrative discretion to hold up the refugee program is distinct from the obligations of the USRAP. We analyze why the court treated the 'Government likely to prevail' factor differently for the Suspension of Admission versus the Defunding of Services, and how publishing these internal predictions in a procedural stay order impacts litigation strategy and the reliability of九寨 travel in the 2025 season. The post also explores the procedural shift from 'Administrative Stays' to 'Scheduled Opinions' and the strategic vacating of prior stays.
